title: Data types, operators, and built-in functions

spans.text: “Data types, operators, and built-in functions” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.

spans.code:
SELECT LOWER('SQL'), ROUND(12.345, 2),
       COALESCE(NULL, 'empty'),
       CAST('42' AS INTEGER),
       7 BETWEEN 1 AND 10 AS in_range;

spans.text: The example returns lowercase sql, rounded 12.35, a fallback text, integer 42; `BETWEEN` is `1` in SQLite/MySQL and `TRUE` in PostgreSQL.

A column's type determines which values it stores and how comparisons work. Use TEXT for text, INTEGER for whole numbers, and integer minor units or DECIMAL/NUMERIC where supported for exact money; date/time types differ between systems. SQL expressions use arithmetic and comparison operators plus AND, OR, NOT, and concatenation such as `||`. Useful built-ins include `LOWER`, `UPPER`, `LENGTH`, `ROUND`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, and `CAST`. SQLite can represent dates as ISO-8601 text, Julian day numbers, or Unix timestamps; PostgreSQL and MySQL also provide date/time types and functions. Function names and date syntax vary by DBMS.

Key line: `SELECT LOWER('SQL'), ROUND(12.345, 2),`
What it does: The example returns lowercase sql, rounded 12.35, a fallback text, integer 42; `BETWEEN` is `1` in SQLite/MySQL and `TRUE` in PostgreSQL.
Why it is used: Do not store money in FLOAT; verify numeric and date functions on the target DBMS.
If omitted or changed: NULL is not an ordinary value: COALESCE picks the first non-NULL value; NULLIF returns NULL when its arguments match.
